26 Electromagnetic waves of frequency 30 THz are in a vacuum.
In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum are the waves?
A
infrared
B
microwave
C
ultraviolet
D
visible light

hints: Convert the prefix: $30 \text{THz} = 30 \times 10^{12} \text{Hz} = 3.0 \times 10^{13} \text{Hz}$ and note the waves travel at $c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{m s}^{-1}$ in vacuum.
Use $c = f\lambda$ to estimate the wavelength for this $10^{13} \text{Hz}$ frequency and think whether it is longer or shorter than red light at about $700 \text{nm}$.
Recall the frequency order around visible light: microwave is below infrared, and infrared is just below visible, while ultraviolet is just above visible.
walkthrough: Write the frequency in standard form: $f = 30 \text{THz} = 30 \times 10^{12} \text{Hz} = 3.0 \times 10^{13} \text{Hz}$.
For all electromagnetic waves in vacuum use $c = f\lambda$ with $c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Compare with known boundaries: visible light is about $400-700 \text{nm}$ or $f \approx 4-8 \times 10^{14} \text{Hz}$, microwaves are about $10^9-10^{11} \text{Hz}$, and ultraviolet is above $10^{15} \text{Hz}$.
A wavelength of $10 \mu\text{m}$ is longer than red light but shorter than microwaves, which is the infrared region. This is option A.

A.explanation: 30 THz gives a wavelength of about $10 \mu\text{m}$, which lies just beyond red light in the infrared region.

B.explanation: Microwaves have much lower frequencies around $10^9$ to $10^{11} \text{Hz}$, so $3.0 \times 10^{13} \text{Hz}$ is too high.

C.explanation: Ultraviolet has higher frequency than visible light at about $10^{15}$ to $10^{16} \text{Hz}$, so 30 THz is too low.

D.explanation: Visible light has frequencies around $4 \times 10^{14}$ to $8 \times 10^{14} \text{Hz}$, about ten times larger than 30 THz.
